directions.notesForExperimenters: Be explicit about API impact. Some measured wins depend on a new public API, which is outside the lean-API goal. Use `select_maps`, `resultset_foreach_consumer.dart`, or a similarly full-consumer benchmark before accepting result-shape changes; setup-only transfer wins are not enough. Exp 158 is a narrow private data-structure win inside RowSchema, not evidence to revive larger ResultSet API changes. Exp 176 extended exp 158's identity fast path to Row.containsKey via a shared RowSchema.containsName helper; the two lookup methods (operator[]/indexOf and containsKey/containsName) now share one identity-then-HashMap path, so any future change to the 32-column cap or the identity scan applies to both. Do not retry the exp 141 ResultSet.forEach override unless a future Dart runtime or workload produces a stable target win with neutral controls. Do not retry Row.values ListBase/getRange/fixed-slice views from JIT row_map_facade output alone; exp 193 showed the JIT values lane can flip between ~3 ms and ~9 ms while AOT cleanly rejects the list view. Compile the focused harness before changing Row.values again. For selectBytes transfer-policy work, include the exp 175 `selectBytes() large bytes` metric so large native-byte payloads stay visible. Exp 183 wired a reclaim path for the bounded RSS high-water exp 174 left as future work: the 1 MB cap trigger + 256 KB last-len guard is what makes the policy safe under back-to-back large reads. Any future tuning should raise the trigger (e.g., 4 MB) before touching the guard. The new Diagnostics.readerJsonBufHighWaterBytes is the reusable signal for any future RSS-sensitive selectBytes work — including the broader measurement-system 'memory profiling harness with per-benchmark RSS acceptance criteria' candidate, which can build on top of it rather than from scratch. Exp 185 adds the public release guard for that signal in `benchmark/suites/sqlite_diagnostics.dart`; keep the `JSON buffer reclaim` row green before changing the selectBytes shrink thresholds or last-len guard. Exp 195 promoted exp 190's per-query `tokens_buf` + `token_offsets` / `token_lens` arrays into the `resqlite_cached_stmt` entry; the exp 190 1-row regression guard sits at the millisecond-reporting floor of `wide_cols.dart` (not noise — wrong harness resolution), and the new `select_bytes_repeated_calls.dart` (1000 calls/sample at µs precision) exposes the win on 1-row × 20-col (−9.2 % / −7.2 %) and 10-row × 20-col (−5.1 % / −2.7 %) across two order-flipped passes. Further selectBytes encoder amortization beyond exp 195 should attach onto the cache entry (per-column type hints, value prefixes) only if a workload shows repeated small selectBytes() with a specific structural pattern dominating wall time; the harness for that work is `select_bytes_repeated_calls.dart`, not `wide_cols.dart`. Exp 194 is the gate for future `SQLITE_FLOAT` JSON-formatting changes: run `select_bytes_real_int_fastpath.dart` and preserve the conservative fallback boundaries for fractional values, huge magnitudes, non-finite values, and negative zero. Do not treat the integral-REAL fast path as evidence to revive broad Ryu/Grisu-style float formatting without a much smaller implementation and a production profile showing fractional REAL cells dominate. For BLOB JSON encoder work, exp 201 rejected quote/framing reservation, exp 216 accepted scalar base64 loop unrolling (4x per trip), exp 218 rejected 8x unrolling, and exp 225 accepted widening the inner lookup to a 12-bit pair table (two 16-bit loads + two 16-bit stores per output-4 group). Use `select_bytes_blob_base64.dart`: 4KB is the payload-throughput gate, 128B/16B are mid-size confirmations, and 3B cells are regression guards. Do not retry wider scalar unroll bodies (exp 218); do not retry a wider LUT beyond exp 225's 4096 x 2 B pair table (a 24-bit table is 16 MiB, well past `.rodata` acceptability). Exp 229 accepts the AArch64/NEON `vqtbl4q_u8` kernel that the exp 225 note named as the next mechanism: 48-byte-block SIMD dispatched on `len >= 48`, scalar 12-bit-LUT fallback for the tail and for non-ARM64 targets. Future BLOB work should now target SSSE3 (`_mm_shuffle_epi8`) on x86_64 to widen platform coverage, or a compiler-flag change, or production-profile evidence that BLOB encode still dominates after the NEON kernel lands. Do not retry an in-lined SIMD body: exp 229 discovered that inlining the NEON kernel into `json_write_base64` degrades the small-input scalar path's code gen; keep new SIMD kernels `noinline` so the small-blob hot path stays byte-identical to the pre-SIMD scalar layout. For TEXT JSON encoder work, exp 202 rejected safe-string quote/payload reservation, while exp 219 accepts direct `\u00XX` emission for unnamed control bytes. Use `select_bytes_text_string_reserve.dart`: the control row is the decision lane for control escape formatting, while safe ASCII and named-escape rows are guards. Future TEXT work should target a different mechanism such as the SWAR escape scan, a measurable copy boundary, or production/profile evidence that TEXT cells dominate encoder wall. Exp 230 rejects shipping a second AArch64/NEON safe-prefix encoder at a 256 B cutoff. It proves fused SIMD classification+copy has substantial headroom at 1 KiB (-34% ASCII, -25% CJK), but its 256 B admission lane failed the preset 15% bar on the order flip. Keep `select_bytes_text_string_reserve.dart`: 256 B safe ASCII is the adoption gate for similarly complex SIMD work, 1 KiB/CJK are confirmations, and early-/late-escape rows guard fallback position. The new `native i64 formatter differential` test group (`resqlite_test_i64_to_str`) is the integer formatter's byte-identity gate. Reader dispatch was round-robin, so all four reader isolates independently paid the prepare, schema build and page warm for the same SQL; making dispatch prefer the worker that served the previous read is worth -33% on a statement's first four executions and ~0 by its eight-thousandth. Before calling a per-statement candidate neutral, measure it on `benchmark/experiments/reader_dispatch_stickiness.dart`'s `first{4,8,32}-newsql` lanes, which mint a fresh SQL string per sample; a steady-state lane structurally cannot see it. Exp 266 also closes two per-read candidates by direct probe (claim 266.4): the per-TEXT-cell `Pointer.asTypedList` view allocation is ~1.35 ns/cell (~1.5% of a text-heavy read), and the per-query `RowSchema` copy across the hop is under 1% of a round trip. Do not retry either. `benchmark/experiments/select_inline_dispatch.dart` (exps 265/269) is a partial gate for read routing, a different question from harnesses that measure only read cost. Keep `mixed6-1k` and `int20-10k` as shared-path controls, not mechanically byte-identical ones: exp 269 changed cap accounting in the worker decoder too. Keep `cap-abort` on a fresh SQL string per sample, and keep `point-under-load` and `concurrent8` for admission. The large-cell guard is `blob1-5mb`; work-before-first-row needs a filtered count or unindexed sort because bare `count(*)` uses `OP_Count`; and `frame-jitter` establishes whether a chain of cheap reads yields. Exp 269 showed even that expanded set was incomplete: one built-in function opcode held the caller for 26-28 ms below every row, payload, VM-step and pre-call stopwatch limit. Run `select_inline_opaque_work.dart` before any future routing prototype, and add cold-prepare, large-TEXT, callback, virtual-table and VFS/busy-stall cases rather than treating post-warmup blob/scan neutrality as a bound. The pattern across exps 239, 265 and 269 is now closed for arbitrary `select()`: neither history and queue predictors nor SQLite work counters can guarantee caller-isolate wall time. Keep worker-first execution unless the API becomes explicitly restricted/synchronous or the mechanism can genuinely preempt inside one SQLite operation. Exp 269 also demonstrated why blanket abort replay, process-global SQL-only schema caching, zero-value kill switches and assert-only transfer invariants need adversarial correctness tests before performance evidence. Before changing any SQL-keyed cache cap, trace exact one-based reuse rank in that cache's actual owner and lifetime; never pool across worker isolates or restarts. Exp 272 does not close the separate `ReaderPool.rowSizeMemoryMax` openCandidate: that map is pool/main-isolate-owned, whereas `cachedSqlUtf8` is worker-isolate-local. Exp 279 closes the vehicle question for the read hop and gives this direction a ruler it did not have. Do not propose another transport: exps 265, 269, 270 and 275 removed the worker four ways and were each rejected on a consequence; exp 279 kept the worker and changed what it IS — a POSIX thread with a `Dart_PostCObject_DL` completion — and it costs 4.28 us per round trip parked on a condvar and 3.18 us spinning against 1.46 us for a Dart isolate, +17.3% end to end on a one-row `selectBytes` and never faster at any size. The only reopen condition is claim 279.2's numerator (a platform where a foreign thread wakes a sleeping isolate for materially less than ~2 us); 'try a better primitive' is not one, because the spinning lane already removed it. What replaces the transport as a target is claim 279.3: a point read's whole transport is 3.22 us of claim 265.1's 6.3 us hop, so the other half is resqlite's own per-request work — `_dispatch`'s row-hint lookup and stamping, request construction, the worker's `resqliteReaderSetBusy` bracket and request-type dispatch, `_WorkerSlot`'s completion handler chain, `_record`, `blobTransfer.materializeCells` — none of it individually measured. Decompose before proposing. `benchmark/experiments/isolate_transport_price.dart` is the gate for anything that changes what crosses the isolate boundary, including any revival of columnar transfer: no database, no native code, seconds to run, and it prices request shape, reply shape and bulk payload separately. Its bytes pair is also a standing design constraint (claim 279.4): the VM charges for a payload's BACKING, not its size — identical 256 KB sends in 9.01 us as a view over malloc'd memory and 43.06 us as a heap `Uint8List`, so any candidate that assembles bytes on the Dart heap before sending pays ~5x and nothing downstream recovers it.

live.text: Routing a `select()` to the calling isolate on the strength of a per-SQL row-count high-water mark is REJECTED, because row count cannot bound main-isolate work along three independent axes. (1) Bytes: one row can be arbitrarily large, `SELECT * FROM photos WHERE id = ?` keeps a permanent high-water mark of 1, and with no hop to serialise for, exp 236's 256 KB blob wrap is suppressed — so a 5 MB image copies straight onto the calling isolate, unchecked. Cost varies per execution of the same statement, so no per-SQL history repairs it. (2) Query cost: `count(*)` over a large table and an unindexed `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10` return few rows after unbounded work, which a result-shape signal cannot see because the work precedes the first row. (3) Scheduling: an inline `select()` returns a `List` rather than a `Future`, so a chain of them drains in microtasks with no event-loop turn — N reads are one uninterruptible block, not N interleavable slices, evidenced by exp 265's own `point1` lane at 200 reads / 427 us. The first draft of the writeup claimed a `~16 us per admitted read` bound; that was the bound for the measured shapes (small integers, short TEXT, indexed lookups, hot cache) stated as though general. Prototype preserved at `archive/exp-265`.

live.text: Reader-pool dispatch stickiness — starting `ReaderPool._dispatch`'s scan at the slot that served the previous read rather than the next one — is worth a reproduced -32.2% on a statement's first four executions, -21.8% on its first eight and -13.2% on its first thirty-two, decaying to -1.6% by the eight-thousandth. In absolute terms four sequential point reads of a fresh statement fall from 58 us to 39 us, and the saving is dominated by a term paid once per statement rather than by a per-read rate: ~19 us across the first four executions, ~22 us across the first eight, ~30 us across the first thirty-two. The mechanism accounts for the magnitude — round-robin makes all four reader connections prepare the statement, build its schema and warm its pages, so the candidate avoids three cycles of roughly 6-9 us each, and the percentage falls because an increasing execution count is what it is divided by. Twenty-four alternating-order lane-isolated AOT passes in two collections of twelve, 121 samples per lane per arm; all 24 passes were faster on `first4-newsql` and `first8-newsql`, 22 of 24 were faster on `first32-newsql`, and the shipped-code collection classified all 12 `first4`/`first8` pass-pairs plus four of six `first32` pairs as REPRODUCED. The other two `first32` pairs reversed sign across the order flip and were marked drift-suspected by `ab_drift_check.dart`.

live.text: Stickiness costs concurrency nothing, because a busy preferred slot falls through to the next exactly as a round-robin scan did. Over 24 passes, four concurrent reads read +1.3%, eight against a four-worker pool (so dispatch parks on `_dispatchWaiters`) +0.2%, and a 60,000-slot result that crosses `sacrificeSlotThreshold` and ends its worker on every sample -0.4% — each sign-flipping between the two collections (`conc4` is -1.4% in one and +1.5% in the other), which is what marks them neutral rather than small. The property is pinned deterministically rather than through the noisy lanes: `test/reader_pool_test.dart` asserts that four reads issued without awaiting leave `availableWorkerCount` at zero, which fails if stickiness ever queues them on one worker.

live.text: A fixed per-(statement, worker) cost is structurally invisible to resqlite's benchmark suite, and this is a property of the suite rather than of any one lane. Every release scenario and every focused harness lane executes one statement from tens to thousands of times per sample, because that is what it takes to resolve a per-read effect at microsecond scale; a cost paid once per statement per worker is divided by that repeat count before it is ever reported. The discriminating instrument is a lane that mints a fresh SQL string per sample (a trailing comment leaves the plan identical) and times its first N executions. Three such lanes at N = 4, 8 and 32 bracket where the fixed term stops mattering, and the monotonic decay across them is stronger evidence for a warm-up mechanism than any single lane's magnitude.

live.text: Two candidate per-read costs on the reader hop are refuted by direct probe and should not be attempted again without a new mechanism. First, the per-TEXT-cell `Pointer.asTypedList` view allocation in `decodeQuery`: decoding 40,000 24-byte cells through one fresh external view each costs 432 us against 378 us through a persistent window with offsets, so the view is ~1.35 ns/cell, about 1.5% of the 10k x (4 INT + 4 TEXT) read exp 251 measured at 3,587 us — and routing the bytes through a native scratch buffer to earn it would add a copy larger than the saving. live.text: A dispatch-policy change can break a reclaim path that is driven by traffic, and `selectBytes` is the case in this codebase. Exp 183's `json_buf` reclaim shrinks a reader connection's serialization buffer when a later, *smaller* read arrives on that same connection; a concurrent burst of large byte reads grows all four readers' buffers, and only the round-robin rotation brings the settling small reads back round to reclaim them. Making every read sticky left the three workers a burst had grown unvisited, and `Diagnostics.readerJsonBufHighWaterBytes` settled at 6.2 MB against the 512 KB the exp 185 release guard allows — a real retention regression that the wall-time harness could not see and the guard caught on its first run. `selectBytes` therefore keeps the pre-266 rotation while `select` sticks. The boundary is structural rather than expedient: the bytes path retains a per-connection buffer whose reclaim is traffic-driven, and the rows path retains nothing per connection. Pinned by a `selectBytes keeps rotating` unit test and by the `bytes-first8-newsql` harness lane, which reads -1.2% (7 of 12 passes faster) as an unchanged path should.

live.text: Dart's async plumbing is a nanosecond-scale cost, not a microsecond-scale one, and resqlite's read prologue is priced accordingly. Measured with no SQLite, no isolates and no resqlite code — a sync completer resolved from a separate microtask, reached through four amounts of plumbing, five AOT runs of 21 samples x 200,000 calls: awaiting an already-resolved future before the real one costs 70.7 ns, and each `async` function that only forwards a future costs 34.6 ns. The prologue `Database.select` -> `ReaderPool.select` -> `ReaderPool._dispatch` -> `_WorkerSlot.request` therefore carried 142.7 ns over a direct await, of which a candidate that makes `Database.select`, `Database.selectBytes` and `_dispatch`'s first scan non-async removes ~108 ns. Divided by what it wraps that is 2.0% of a 5.4 us point read, 1.1% of a 20-row page, 0.05% of a 1,000-row read and 0.004% of a sacrificed 10,000-row one — a ceiling below the 5% decision gate on every shape resqlite measures, so no implementation of the idea can clear it. Exp 171 estimated the same resolved-future hop at 1-2 us per call and derived 6-12% of headroom from that estimate; the figure is 14-28x too large and the headroom never existed.

live.text: Running a read on a native POSIX thread instead of a Dart reader isolate is slower, not faster, and the primitive is not the reason. An awaited Dart isolate round trip costs 1.46 us; handing the same job to a worker thread and getting an answer back through `Dart_PostCObject_DL` costs 4.28 us parked on a condvar and 3.18 us with the worker spinning on the queue (a burned core, included so the result cannot be blamed on the wake primitive). End to end against a real database the same shape holds: `db.selectBytes()` on one row is 5.48 us against 6.43 us for the native worker (+17.3%), at 1,000 rows 246.5 against 249.3 (+1.1%), and at 5,000 rows 1239 against 1233 (-0.5%, inside the floor). Native dispatch is never faster at any size. The vehicle question is therefore closed: keeping SQLite off the calling isolate does not cost extra because a Dart isolate was chosen.

live.text: The 2-3 us by which native dispatch loses is the cross-thread wake, not the native port. A post issued from the calling thread itself, so the main isolate never sleeps between issuing and receiving, costs 0.67 us — `Dart_PostCObject_DL` delivery plus one event-loop turn. Everything above that in the native lanes is the OS scheduling round trip, and the Dart VM performs the equivalent handoff in both directions for 1.46 us. This is the number that makes the rejection conditional rather than permanent: a runtime or SDK where a foreign thread can wake a sleeping isolate cheaply would change the arithmetic, and nothing else in the mechanism would have to change.

live.text: A point read's cross-isolate transport is 3.22 us — about half of claim 265.1's 6.3 us hop. Measured with no SQLite and no resqlite code, one persistent echo isolate, changing only what crosses the boundary: an int each way is 1.46 us, a `SelectRequest`-shaped object outbound adds 0.50 us, a point read's reply shape inbound (one row of six cells, six column names, the `(result, sacrificed, error)` envelope, pre-built on the worker) adds 1.74 us, and both together in one trip are 3.22 us — less than the 3.70 us the parts sum to, because some of what each shape costs is per-trip rather than per-payload, which is why the combined lane exists. The remaining ~3.1 us of the hop is resqlite's own per-request work on the two sides of the messages — pool bookkeeping and the row-size memory lookup, request construction, the worker's `setBusy` bracket and request dispatch, the completion handler chain, blob materialization — none of which a transport change touches. Any future candidate in this direction should be aimed at that half; the messages have at most 3.22 us in them.

live.text: What `SendPort.send` charges for a bulk payload is its backing, not its size. Byte-for-byte identical 256 KB costs 9.01 us to send as a view over malloc'd memory and 43.06 us as an ordinary heap `Uint8List` — 4.8x, reproduced in every pass of two collections with the two lanes differing in nothing else. This is the measurement behind exp 174's choice to send a `Uint8List` view over the reader's persistent `json_buf` rather than materialize the result first, and it generalises past `selectBytes`: any path that assembles bytes on the Dart heap before sending them pays roughly five times the transfer. It is the bulk-payload counterpart to claim 245.1's copy-per-slot rule for result structure.

live.text: Copying is a wash between the two transports, so external typed data buys only what it saves by not copying at all — and that variant is not implementable. A malloc plus a 256 KB `memcpy` on the native side costs 6.28 us (`nport-bytes` 11.91 minus `nport-bytes-nocopy` 5.63); the VM's copy of the same view costs 7.55 us (`iso-bytes` 9.01 minus `iso-echo` 1.46). The realistic native variant therefore loses by 2.90 us, which is its dispatch penalty and nothing else. Posting the buffer itself with no copy is 3.38 us faster than the shipped path, but making that real means handing `json_buf` to the main isolate and giving the connection a fresh one, forfeiting the buffer reuse exp 174 measured as decisive (a `NativeFinalizer` zero-copy transfer was 14-24% slower at every size) and the shrink-and-reclaim policy exp 183 built on it. The prize is 1.4% of a 1,000-row `selectBytes` against a fixed dispatch tax on every small read.

directions.currentRead: Several plausible optimizations failed because the benchmark did not stress the target path or because run noise hid small effects. Measurement work can be the highest-signal experiment when it unlocks a named implementation or rejection decision, but scheduled runners should first look for an instrument-and-implement path. Exp 119/121/136/147 are the recent stream-dispatch examples: exp 119 located surviving dispatch pressure in stream admission, exp 121 ruled out invalidation traversal as a wall-time target (10–15% of overlap wall, intersection ~3–6%), exp 136 added the completion-side reader-handler counter plus drain-aware audit snapshots and found 28.57% of A11c overlap total wall in the reader worker port handler chain at ~18 us per call, and exp 147 added the writer SQLite wall split and found SQLite-facing writer calls are not the active stream-fanout bottleneck on A11c overlap or keyed-PK. Exp 143 confirmed the pinned Tracelite profile path is useful because it captures dispatch floors, floor-subtracted work, memory diagnostics, allocation counters, source provenance, and graph data in one run; exp 169 consumes its interpretation gap by validating that `tracelite explain` emits workload-summary insight IDs for dispatch floors, work-bound operations, tail spread, RSS, allocation, and WAL signal before the profile wrapper completes. Exp 161 closes the matching release-suite gap for the writer side by promoting exp 159's concurrent-burst shape into `benchmark/suites/writes.dart` as a paired Single Inserts (sequential) / Concurrent Single Inserts (concurrent) row pair; the resqlite concurrent median (~1.1 ms) is now ~60% below the sequential median (~2.9 ms) on a public lane, and future writer-scheduling experiments can claim release-suite wins without depending on the focused `writer_pipelining.dart` script. Exp 177 mechanizes the JOURNAL's order-flipped drift check: `cvPct` + `classifyDriftFlag` in `benchmark/shared/stats.dart` and a `benchmark/ab_drift_check.dart` CLI classify a phase-ordered A/B regression flag as reproduced / drift-suspected / inconclusive from two order-flipped passes of per-run values, reproducing the manual verdicts on the recorded exp 159 (CV asymmetry) and exp 167 (sign reversal) flags. It is methodology tooling (exp 161 / 169 class), not a wall-time change, so future A/B runners can cite a deterministic verdict instead of re-deriving the CV-asymmetry rule each time. Exp 178 closes a silent pipeline gap on the experiment->chart linker itself: `generate_history.dart` already failed the build when an Accepted experiment linked a baseline-shaped run while a candidate existed (`_assertAcceptedExperimentsLinkToCandidates`), but it tolerated the more common case — a chartable experiment with NO linked run and NO `**Benchmark Run:**` opt-out, which silently drops off the chart when a runner forgets the result file or mismatches its date. A structural tally on main showed only ~5 of 23 null-run accepted/in-review experiments declared the opt-out. Exp 178 adds `_assertNewExperimentsLinkOrDeclareRun` (over a pure `findUndeclaredMissingRunExperiments` detector) that fails the build for accepted/in-review experiments numbered >= 178 with a null run and no opt-out declaration; pre-178 experiments are grandfathered via a cutoff constant (same pattern as `experimentEntriesRequiredFrom`). No runtime code, history.json unchanged. Exp 214 adds `benchmark/experiments/write_result_direct_read.dart`, a focused µs/call public writer harness for scalar writer-result handling. Its first use rejected direct pointer reads of `resqlite_write_result` because the order-flipped A/B did not reproduce a stable win; keep the harness as a guardrail, not as an invitation to stack writer-result micro-optimizations. Exp 261 adds the memory half of the focused-harness toolkit (benchmark/shared/memory_probe.dart). The instrument is fixed by a constraint rather than chosen: an AOT binary exposes no VM service, so heap and allocation profiles are unavailable in the only mode exp 193 permits for decode-path results, and ProcessInfo is all there is. Gate on maxRss with one process per lane — a sampled currentRss peak reported +75% about the same change maxRss reported as -1.7%, because retention on this codebase is dominated by sacrificed reader isolates returning their pages rather than by the change under test. Its sensitivity is now known and is low: peak read-path memory held within ~1 MB from v0.3.0 to exp 259 across ~40 merged experiments while wall time fell 25-40%, so this guard catches a doubling, not a 5% drift. Exp 262 closes the RSS-acceptance-criteria candidate that had been open since 2026-05-02, and fixes why the trend charts are sparse. The thresholds were never missing — generateMemoryComparison has rendered per-benchmark bootstrap-MDE thresholds and a regression marker all along — so compareMemory now returns the counts and regressed names beside the table, and --fail-on-memory-regression exits non-zero (opt-in; whether CI passes it is a maintainer decision). The larger fix is granularity: #282 persisted per completed repeat, but the sqlite_async peer segfault fires at the Memory scenario inside repeat 1, so no repeat ever completed and exps 260 and 261 each ran fourteen scenarios and produced nothing. The suite now persists per scenario, with repeatCount counting only finished repeats and scenariosCompleted/scenarioTotal/partial marking the shortfall so a partial run self-excludes from trends. A SIGKILL at scenario 10 of 16 preserves 9 scenarios and 153 metrics where nothing survived before. Exp 263 adds the rule that makes exp 261's instrument interpretable: a memory lane must state whether it measures one live result or what a repeatedly-reading process retains. RSS never falls, so 26 reads accumulate 26 results of garbage — the same 10k-row lane reads 99 MB one way and 36.1 MB the other, a 2.7x difference with no code change between them. benchmark/experiments/select_memory_decomposition.dart runs both configurations and reports which it used.

directions.notesForExperimenters: It is valid for a scheduled run to improve measurement rather than implementation only when the missing signal is the bottleneck and the same branch cannot reasonably run the candidate it enables. Use the Tracelite profile wrapper before adding a legacy profile harness: exp 143 shows the structured artifacts already expose dispatch-vs-work and memory/allocation shape, and exp 169 makes the generated insight layer a required profile artifact instead of a manual JSON inspection step. If profile data still answers a question only after manual inspection, prefer improving Tracelite explanation rules or the Resqlite wrapper guard over duplicating the measurement path. For scoped resqlite counters, start them as temporary instrumentation inside the performance branch; keep them only when future experiments will reuse the counter or it replaces a weaker legacy path. Exp 136 is the main-isolate pattern: add the counter, snapshot inside the shared `audit_workloads.dart` scenario runners with both at-burst-end and post-drain snapshots, and have the harness pick the right one for its question. Exp 147 is the writer-isolate pattern: time the writer-side slice in the worker and aggregate it back through responses. Exp 178 added a build-time guard against silently-unmapped chartable experiments; if you legitimately have no release run (Tracelite A/B or focused harness), declare it with a `**Benchmark Run:**` header (`none` / `n/a` / `tracelite ...`) or the generator will fail. To pull older unmapped experiments under the guard, backfill their headers and lower `_benchmarkRunDeclarationCutoff` in the same change.

live.text: Dart's async plumbing is a nanosecond-scale cost, not a microsecond-scale one, and resqlite's read prologue is priced accordingly. Measured with no SQLite, no isolates and no resqlite code — a sync completer resolved from a separate microtask, reached through four amounts of plumbing, five AOT runs of 21 samples x 200,000 calls: awaiting an already-resolved future before the real one costs 70.7 ns, and each `async` function that only forwards a future costs 34.6 ns. The prologue `Database.select` -> `ReaderPool.select` -> `ReaderPool._dispatch` -> `_WorkerSlot.request` therefore carried 142.7 ns over a direct await, of which a candidate that makes `Database.select`, `Database.selectBytes` and `_dispatch`'s first scan non-async removes ~108 ns. Divided by what it wraps that is 2.0% of a 5.4 us point read, 1.1% of a 20-row page, 0.05% of a 1,000-row read and 0.004% of a sacrificed 10,000-row one — a ceiling below the 5% decision gate on every shape resqlite measures, so no implementation of the idea can clear it. Exp 171 estimated the same resolved-future hop at 1-2 us per call and derived 6-12% of headroom from that estimate; the figure is 14-28x too large and the headroom never existed.

Copies (2) and (3) are irreducible; copy (1)'s cost is not the copy itself but its destination.

Wrapping large blob params in `TransferableTypedData` is a reproduced ~15-20% end-to-end win on 256 KB-512 KB single-row blob INSERTs (256 KB -16.4%/-22.7%, 512 KB -10.4%/-11.8% across order-flipped passes; every 256/512 KB leg candidate-faster across ~7 passes, sub-threshold controls flip sign as noise). The win is size-bounded and the bounds are mechanistic, not incidental. Below ~256 KB the direct graph copy takes its fast path (new-space alloc + one unchunked memmove, ~15% over a plain copy) while the wrap still pays malloc/finalizer/materialize bookkeeping — measured +23% at 64 KB transport. At >= 1 MB two things converge: SQLite's WAL write dominates the insert, and very large payloads allocate straight to old space, skipping the new-space churn that drives the mid-size win — so end-to-end goes neutral (never negative; the wrap still trims main-isolate blocking, hence a threshold floor with no ceiling). Large direct sends additionally abort onto `CopyTypedDataBaseWithSafepointChecks` (100 KB safepoint-polled chunks, ~2x a plain memcpy at >= 1 MB), a deliberate VM trade of copy throughput for isolate-group responsiveness. changedBeliefs: The `Isolate.exit` sacrifice policy (kill the reader to zero-copy a >=256 KB result heap instead of paying the SendPort graph copy) was re-evaluated against the Dart 2.15 isolate-group send model, where SendPort.send SHARES immutable leaves (strings/ints/canonical) and only COPIES the mutable structural graph. Confirmed transport model (`native_vs_heap_send.dart`): send cost tracks the mutable/copyable payload — a heap Uint8List send blows up with size (203-272 us at 512-731 KB) while a native-backed view sends cheaply (23-44 us). So send is cheap exactly when the result is immutable-heavy (text) or externally backed, and expensive only for large mutable structure.

Sacrifice-vs-send crossover (A/B via a reverted RESQLITE_SACRIFICE_THRESHOLD define): on a numeric lane (structure-only, slots = rows x cols) send is faster-or-level up to ~20k slots and sacrifice edges ahead only above ~32k slots by a noisy ~3-4% (2000/8000/20000/32000/48000 slots: sacrifice 76.8/238.6/976.5/1194.8/1856.3 vs send 72.3/226.3/931.9/1233.8/1932.6). On a text lane (200 B strings) send wins everywhere and large (1000 rows: 149.4 vs 438.3 us) because strings are shared on send while sacrifice pays a respawn for a copy it never needed. The crossover metric is STRUCTURAL SLOT COUNT, not bytes.

Neither candidate change survives. Retiring sacrifice (send-always) is rejected because send-always would regress the high-structural-count tail (>= ~32k slots) where sacrifice still wins. Re-triggering on structural slot count instead of estimated bytes is rejected because the crossover sits at a high slot count with a ~3-4% noisy margin and estimated bytes already correlates with slot count for structural results — the accounting complexity isn't paid for. Current 256 KB estimated-byte policy stands unchanged.

Measurement confound identified: within one process the repeated sacrifice respawns accumulate and interfere, so a per-process A/B cannot cleanly isolate a single sacrifice-vs-send at a fixed size — it biases the sacrifice lane by respawn history. This is why the send-vs-sacrifice signal has stayed muddy across exp 241's harnesses (and why the stranded `sacrifice_reeval_ab.dart`, which also lost its `debugReaderSpawnCount` counter to exp 236's cleanup, could not resolve it).
nextSignals: Sacrifice retirement/retuning is REJECTED but not closed. Reopen only with a clean SINGLE-SHOT per-process sacrifice-vs-send harness (one fresh measurement per process, no respawn accumulation) that removes the confound documented here — if that still shows send winning at the high-structural tail (>= ~32k slots), send-always becomes viable. Do not re-run the per-process accumulating A/B expecting a cleaner answer; it structurally can't give one.

A production profile showing real result-size/shape distribution would settle it faster than more microbenchmarks: if results cluster in the send-favored range (text-heavy, or < ~32k structural slots) and sacrifice is firing on the 256 KB byte threshold anyway, that is direct evidence to lower or retire the threshold. The byte threshold is a proxy; the real cost driver is structural slot count of the MUTABLE graph.

General result-transfer-shape rule reinforced: send is cheap for immutable-heavy (shared leaves) and native/external-backed content, expensive only for large mutable structure. Sacrifice pays off only when the mutable structural graph is large enough that the copy exceeds a reader respawn — a narrow, high-slot-count regime, not a general large-result regime.

changedBeliefs: Exp 234's per-occurrence blob-param wrapping carried a latent aliasing regression: `wrapBlobParams` called `TransferableTypedData.fromList` once per qualifying position, so a caller passing the SAME `Uint8List` object to N positions (or reusing one buffer across a coalesced `MultiExecuteRequest` burst) got N independent external copies of one buffer. That is strictly worse than the graph copy exp 234 replaced, because `SendPort.send`'s object-graph copy preserves reference identity and would have copied the shared buffer once. The regression is invisible on single-reference writes (the common case) and only bites when one buffer is referenced multiple times in a send.

The fix is the 'table protocol': wrap by identity via an identity-keyed cache (`HashMap(equals: identical, hashCode: identityHashCode)`), sharing ONE `TransferableTypedData` per unique backing buffer referenced at every occurrence. The graph copier sends the shared wrapper once (identity preserved across the hop); the writer materializes each unique wrapper exactly once (a second `materialize()` throws), so `unwrapBlobParams` dedups by wrapper identity and `_handleMultiExecute` threads one shared unwrap cache across the envelope's writes. Distinct buffers are unchanged (each still gets its own wrapper); the no-large-blob fast path still returns the input list with no allocation.

Isolated transport (one 300 KB buffer referenced N times, `alias_transfer_isolated.dart`) ranks three wrapping shapes and the table protocol dominates at every N: table 32.9/27.0/28.2/33.8/56.5 us at N=1/2/4/8/32 (flat); baseline (N TTD) 44.4/49.6/70.8/132.0/1502.7 us (linear blowup — the regression, ~27x table at N=32); census (leave aliased on the graph copy) ~180-210 us flat (one copy, but the large HEAP blob aborts onto the chunked `CopyTypedDataBaseWithSafepointChecks` slow path AND re-lands on the GC heap — the exact cost exp 234 exists to avoid). Table = baseline's single fast external copy + census's shared-once transport, with neither downside, and peak external memory drops from N buffers to 1. Table even edges baseline at N=1 (same single wrap; the gap is noise).

The table protocol is a write-envelope concern and does NOT transfer to reads: a read response's blob cells are distinct materialized objects with no caller aliasing to collapse (exp 236 handles read-cell transfer). Do not add an identity-dedup layer to the read path looking for a symmetric win — the shape that makes table pay off (one caller object referenced N times) does not exist there.

changedBeliefs: Invalidation-grouped rerun batching does NOT help reactive fan-out, and specifically regresses the metric that matters. It was implemented internally (SelectIfChangedBatchRequest + worker loop, ReaderPool.selectBatchIfChanged, batched StreamEngine._flushQueue/_requeryBatch, lastRowCount cost-gate) with no public API change. Clean cross-worktree A/B (two binaries, 3 alternated rounds, warm regime) measured single-write emission latency SLOWER on every lane: homogeneous +22% p50 / +59% p95, heterogeneous +66% p50 / +52% p95. The mechanism: a batched reply is indivisible, so the one changed stream's fresh result is delivered only when its whole batch finishes — it waits behind ~24 cheap unchanged batch-mates' re-hashes. Message-count amortization is the wrong lever for a latency-bound workload. This is the third rejection of the same trade (exp 148 reduced completion callbacks but regressed measured elapsed; exp 239 rejected shared indivisible replies). The lastRowCount cost-gate keeps a large partition off the critical path but not the common many-small-partitions wait.

For dispatch/scheduling/isolate-message changes, trust only cross-worktree (or the tracelite two-root wrapper); a single-process toggle delta is suspect regardless of what the drift classifier says.

The stream fan-out latency workload was previously unmeasured end-to-end for the suppressed-rerun case. `high_cardinality_fanout`'s settle returns after a fixed 200 ms quiet window keyed on emission counts, so when 99 of 100 reruns suppress their emission (the dominant case) it never waits for those reruns to drain — its 'write burst' number is write dispatch + a constant, not rerun-processing cost. `stream_rerun_latency.dart` (single-write, per-emit completer) is the lane that actually exposes fan-out emission latency, and it is what made this rejection visible.
nextSignals: Do not retry invalidation-grouped rerun batching as a latency play. The batched reply is indivisible, so any grouping delays the one result a subscriber waits on behind its batch-mates — reproduced against a clean baseline here. Reuse the cross-worktree A/B for any stream-dispatch or reader-message change; do not accept a single-process toggle delta. `stream_rerun_latency.dart` is the durable single-write fan-out emission-latency gate (homogeneous small partitions + heterogeneous large/small); run it on baseline and candidate worktrees. The reader pool is 4 workers and each worker's connection steps one query at a time, so a 100-stream fan-out already serializes into ~25 waves regardless of message shape — the reruns are latency-bound on the serial connection, not on the pool. The off-writer mechanism retains substantial local value once the storm is fixed. First threshold-crossing p50 improves 53.0% / 63.9% across the order flip, and foreground reads improve as well, confirming that inline PASSIVE ownership is a real latency ceiling when the crossing occurs.

Reset/high-water gating is not sufficient for sustained health because SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE is best-effort. A checkpoint may return SQLITE_OK with only partial progress; consuming that attempt without bounded retry can leave a burst with no future commit to create another high-water request. Two candidate repeats strand 9,165 / 10,316 pending frames, while sustained awaited 8 KiB writes regress +152.5% / +138.1% at p50, +148.8% / +163.0% at p95, and +203.9% / +161.7% at p99.

If the first commit after restart lands equal to or above the prior observed count but below the next high-water, the candidate cannot identify the new generation and can leave an already-above-threshold WAL unscheduled. The preserved first-crossing and read wins do not repay the current lifecycle surface without incidence evidence: a second keyed writable connection, dedicated isolate and SendPort, three private FFI calls, mutex-protected request/high-water state, worker-failure propagation, error and partial-progress handling, and cross-sender close draining are all required for a behavior whose representative user frequency remains unknown. changedBeliefs: The Dart row decoder was paying to answer a question C already had the inputs for. `fastDecodeText` had to classify every TEXT cell as ASCII (Latin-1 widen) or not (utf8.decode) before it could build the String, costing a second ExternalTypedData word view plus a bounds-checked scan per cell — and falling back to a byte-by-byte loop for values under 16 bytes or on an unaligned pointer, which covers most real database text. `resqlite_step_row` holds the same pointer and length one frame earlier, in cache, where the answer is a branch-free SWAR pass.

Moving the classification into the native step loop (RESQLITE_TEXT_ASCII = type code 6) is worth a reproduced 10-24% on text-bearing select() reads, including 19-24% on the repo's canonical 6-column mixed product row, across two order-flipped AOT passes. The saving is per TEXT cell, so it scales with text carried per read rather than with row count; the 400 B lane gains most (-22.2% / -19.4%) because the replaced Dart scan walked ~50 words per cell, and the canonical mixed row gains as much as it does because its description column is ~85 bytes on its own.

Scanning a non-ASCII value all the way to the end in C, instead of bailing at the first high byte, costs nothing measurable: ordinary CJK text moved -2.4% / -1.7% and the worst case built to expose the trade (400 B with its one multibyte character at byte 0) moved +1.1% / -1.0%. The full-scan shape buys a single branch on the common all-ASCII path, and any value that fails the test is about to be walked again by utf8.decode at roughly ten times the per-byte cost. This is the counterpoint to exp 235's abandon-on-first-miss lesson — there the fast path was abandoned for the whole remainder; here the 'miss' path is a separate, more expensive decoder that re-reads the value regardless.

This does not reopen exp 258's columnar rewrite or exp 251's decode-bottleneck premise. Both closed on the grounds that a storage-shape change moves work between isolates rather than removing it; this removes work outright and is orthogonal to where the result is stored.

The decode loop's remaining Dart-side per-cell work is the ExternalTypedData view and the String copy itself; both are VM-owned, so further gains here need a Dart runtime change (a native UTF-8 String entry point, or a non-allocating Pointer view), not another resqlite-side move.

changedBeliefs: Growing `decodeQuery`'s `List<Object?>` is not amortised-free, and it is the single largest Dart-side cost of a large read. A standalone AOT reproduction of the decode loop over a fixed cell buffer measures 2318 us for the doubling path against 865 us pre-sized on 10k x 20 INTEGER, with loads + switch + stores together under 500 us. That lands within 8% of exp 251's 2524 us of `Dart result construction` on the same shape, so the bucket exp 251 refused to design against is mostly buffer growth rather than cell decoding. Growth costs what it costs because a `List<Object?>` grow copies every live element with a store barrier into a freshly faulted array; a 200k-slot result copies ~322k slots through ~5 MB of transient garbage.

Exp 059 rejected this mechanism for the wrong reason and with a design defect. Its stated grounds were the April release suite's noise floor and medians taken across iterations; its mechanism claim (`list growth is already cheap`, `only ~3-4 growths`) counts growths rather than slots copied and is false; and it sized the *initial* allocation from the hint, which is precisely the change exp 067 measured as a 40-44% regression on small-query workloads the same day. A win on large reads and a regression on small ones nets to the noise it reported.

A per-isolate cache is not a durable place for anything a large read teaches. Results over `sacrificeSlotThreshold` (32768 slots) return via `Isolate.exit` and end the worker that produced them, so a hint kept in the worker's schema cache is discarded exactly when the result was large enough to need it, and otherwise describes only the executions that landed on one of four pool workers. Measured directly: the worker-local version won 30-35% on sub-threshold reads and ~1% on the 200k-slot lane. Moving the memory to `ReaderPool` and stamping it on the request took the same lane to -25%.

A size hint must be applied where a wrong answer cannot cost anything. Applied to the initial allocation, a hint saturated by a `SELECT ... LIMIT ?` statement's large leg made its 50-row leg 2.8x slower (68 -> 198 us) — zero-filling 60000 unused slots costs more than the doubling it removes. Applied at the growth step the same lane is neutral by construction, because a result that fits in the initial buffer never reaches the code. This is a stronger guarantee than a floor: it makes the whole mechanism unreachable for small results rather than merely conservative.

Per-request bookkeeping on the main isolate is measurable on a point read. The first version's two map lookups per request cost ~0.3 us, about 6% of a point query, attributed by building a variant with the pool bookkeeping removed and watching the lane return to baseline. Reading the entry once per request and never creating one for a SQL that has not exceeded the initial buffer brought it under the 3% effect floor.

claims.text: Sizing `decodeQuery`'s result buffer from a main-isolate memory of what the same SQL returned before — applied at the first growth, never to the initial allocation — is worth a reproduced -25.1% / -24.8% on 10k x 20 INTEGER, -32.2% / -33.7% on 5k x 4 INTEGER, and -33.6% / -32.3% on the repo's canonical 6-column product row at 10k rows (3.5 ms -> 2.3 ms), measured end to end through the public `select()`. Both controls (200-row and point reads, which never reach the growth path) move opposite signs inside the 3% floor, and both mispredict guards are neutral.

Exp 067 attributed its regressions to a VM fast path that makes one large null-filled list cheaper *per slot* than a small one. That is true and it does not support the conclusion: a standalone AOT reproduction of the allocation shape measures 1,536 slots at 0.28 ns/slot against 12 slots at 1.8 ns/slot, so the large allocation is six times cheaper per slot and twenty times more expensive in total. What actually made exp 067 regress was growth, not allocation, and exp 260 has since supplied the thing that lets the shrink avoid growth: a per-SQL memory of how many rows each statement returns. Conditioned on that memory and clamped so it can only ever shrink, the initial allocation is worth a reproduced 7.4% on the canonical 6-column point read and 27.4% on a 21-column one.

A buffer-size hint that can *under*-predict must be a high-water mark, not a sliding window, and this is the single most transferable thing the run produced. Exp 260's growth hint takes the smaller of a SQL's last two row counts, which is right for growth because over-sizing is the expensive mistake there. A high-water mark cannot repeat. What it gives up is a statement that was once large and is now permanently small, which keeps today's allocation forever.

The cost of a mispredict is a one-off +1.6%, and it is bounded by arithmetic rather than by measurement. The doubling chain's landing point depends on where it starts, so an undershoot can be favourable (`undershoot-jump`, 5,000 rows: from 25 rows the chain lands on 6,400, from 256 it lands on 8,192) or adverse (`undershoot-mid`, 3,300 rows: 6,400 against 4,096, four extra growths and 56% over-allocation). changedBeliefs: The `select() round-trip floor` has been the terminal argument in this direction for months and was never a measurement. Claim 258.2 rejected a columnar result store partly because its sub-threshold transfer saving was `below the round-trip floor`; exp 264 put a point read at `5-8 us, most of which is the isolate round trip`; exps 209 and 239 both went after the floor by amortising a hop across several queries. It is now priced: on the canonical 6-column point read the hop is 6.3 us of an 8.4 us read, and removing it leaves 2.1 us. So the floor was real, it was most of a small read, and it is not a floor — it is a routing decision. Everything previously rejected as `below the round-trip floor` was measured against a denominator four times larger than the work it was competing with. This survives the candidate's rejection and is the run's lasting contribution.

Rows returned cannot bound main-isolate work, and this is why the candidate was rejected rather than shipped. It fails along three independent axes, each sufficient on its own. (1) One row can be arbitrarily large: `SELECT * FROM photos WHERE id = ?` has a permanent high-water mark of 1, is admitted forever, and — because there is no hop — has exp 236's blob wrapping suppressed, so a 5 MB image is copied straight onto the calling isolate. Cost also varies per *execution* of the same statement (id=1 a thumbnail, id=2 a raw), so no per-SQL history predicts the next parameter. (2) Rows returned is not query cost: `count(*)` over a large table and an unindexed `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10` both return few rows after unbounded work, and a result-shape signal is blind to work that happens before the first row. (3) Inline reads never yield, so N of them coalesce into one uninterruptible block rather than N interleavable ones. Any future routing policy must treat row count as an efficiency hint and never as a safety bound.

A guard set derived from the lanes you already have tests the hypothesis you already believe. Exp 265's nine lanes were all small integers and short TEXT, cheap indexed lookups, hot page cache — and every kill condition tested whether the *hint* was wrong about row count, which is the one failure mode the row cap already handled. The three real failure modes needed lanes that did not exist and that nobody would build while the happy path was reading -75%. The discriminating lanes are cheap and specific: a one-row read of a 5 MB blob, a `count(*)` over a large table, and a frame-shaped workload rather than a throughput one.

A safety property must be enforced, not predicted, and exp 265 contains one of each so the contrast is exact. The row cap predicts nothing — it aborts mid-decode and falls back, and it is correct whether or not the hint was right (+24.7% once per statement, claim 265.4). The eligibility test predicts, and every one of its failure modes is unbounded. The fix is two more enforcement points rather than a better predictor: `sqlite3_column_bytes` gives a cell's size before anything is copied into Dart (and the value is already loaded at the line where the wrap branch is skipped), and `sqlite3_progress_handler` interrupts every N VM steps. With both, the high-water hint stops being load-bearing and becomes what it is good at — avoiding wasted aborts.

The cost of the hop is not only its own latency but the queue in front of it, and no transfer-shaped analysis in this direction could see that. Exps 244/245/246 measured intrinsic transfer with a prepared-result barrier and pool capacity with a burst, both correctly, and both hold the *request* constant. A point read issued while four 1,000-row reads occupy every worker waits 533-1169 us against 37-52 us for one that never enters the queue. When the next runner asks what a scheduling change is worth, the lane has to contend for the pool; a lane that has the pool to itself measures the smaller half of the answer. This is independent of the rejection and applies to exp 266's stickiness and anything after it.

Losing the pool's parallelism costs a caller nothing at point-read sizes. Eight distinct point reads issued together run four-wide across four workers and strictly serially when the caller runs them itself, and serial is 70% faster, reproduced in both pairs of both collections. Four workers cannot make up a per-request overhead larger than the request. This bounds the pool's value precisely — it is worth having for results large enough that decode dominates dispatch, and it is a tax below that — and it holds whatever routing policy is eventually used to act on it.

Keep `mixed6-1k` and `int20-10k`: both return more rows than any plausible cap, so they run byte-identical code in both arms and read a cross-worktree binary offset directly (the exp 254 trap). Keep `cap-abort` on a fresh SQL string per sample, since an abort is once-per-statement and any other construction leaves the lane inert after its first sample. Keep `point-under-load` and `concurrent8`, which measure admission rather than transfer. Then add the three lanes exp 265 lacked before trusting any successor: a one-row read returning a 5 MB blob, a `count(*)` over a large table, and a frame-shaped workload that can see microtask coalescing. The first two fail against `archive/exp-265`.

Any successor to exp 265 must enforce rather than predict. `sqlite3_column_bytes` reports a cell's size before it is copied into Dart, and the value is already loaded at the line where the blob-wrap branch is skipped, so a running byte cap is one comparison. `sqlite3_progress_handler` interrupts every N VM steps and bounds the cases where work precedes the first row. Neither addresses microtask coalescing — an inline read returns a `List`, not a `Future`, so it never yields — and that needs a per-drain time budget, which is a design question rather than a guard. A candidate that solves two of the three is not ready.

Exp 239 was rejected because queue depth cannot encode query cost; exp 265 because row count cannot either. The generalisation is worth stating once so a third experiment does not rediscover it: no signal derived from a query's *shape* or its *position in a queue* bounds its cost, because the expensive part can precede the first row and can hide inside one cell. The signals that do bound cost are the ones SQLite computes while running — VM steps, column bytes — and they are only available mid-flight, which forces an abort-and-retry structure rather than an admission test.

Stream reruns look like the obvious next application of inline routing and are not a shortcut around this rejection: `selectIfChanged` on an unchanged result is a C hash pass with no Dart decode, the cheapest thing the pool carries and so the largest relative hop, but an unchanged result is still produced by a query whose cost row count cannot predict. All three of claim 265.6's failure modes apply unchanged. If it is attempted, exp 249's rule holds — A/B across worktrees on `benchmark/experiments/stream_rerun_latency.dart`, never with an in-process toggle.

Exp 265's collections were taken on a host at 0-39% CPU idle with load average near 37, none of it the run's doing, which is the second consecutive experiment under claim 264.6's conditions. The order-flipped design and the two mechanically-inert controls carried it — controls at +0.1% and +3.2% against primaries of -35% to -95% — but exp 264's proposed fix still stands unbuilt: sample idle CPU at lane start and print it beside the medians, so a reader can see the host's state without taking the runner's word for it.

changedBeliefs: `dart run tool/knowledge/impact.dart origin/main` reports no recorded belief retired or transitively unsupported by this run, and that is correct: nothing here contradicts a prior claim. What it adds is a cost class the direction had no vocabulary for. Every read-path claim from exp 251 onward is a *per-read* rate — nanoseconds per cell, microseconds per request, a fraction of transfer versus decode — and each was measured on a lane that executes one statement thousands of times, which is the only way to resolve a rate. A fixed per-(statement, worker) cost is invisible in that regime by construction, and this run measures one at roughly 18 us: the prepare, schema build and page warm each of four reader isolates pays independently for a statement the first one has already run. Read alongside claim 264.1 and claim 260.1, both of which are real and both of which are per-read: they describe the cost of the ten-thousandth execution of a statement, and this describes the cost of its first.

The reader pool's round-robin was never a load-balancing decision that anyone measured; it was the obvious way to write a scan, and it has been in place since exp 011 built the persistent pool. Exp 030 optimised what a worker does once it is chosen (dedicated reader indices, no C pool mutex) and exp 105 sized the pool, but which idle worker an idle pool picks had never been an experiment. It is worth about a third of a statement's first four executions, so the general belief to carry forward is that a policy nobody has measured is not the same as a policy that has been validated — especially one whose cost is structurally invisible to the suite that would have caught it.

Peak RSS moves with warm-state duplication, in the direction that makes the mechanism legible from a second angle. `first4-newsql` reads 27.0 -> 26.1 MB and `first8-newsql` 29.6 -> 28.1 MB, while the sacrificing lane holds at 95.9 -> 96.0. Four connections each holding a prepared statement, a cached schema and warmed pages for the same SQL is four copies of state one worker now holds once. Consistent with claim 263's account of where resqlite's footprint actually sits — the pool, not the row representation — and a small argument that pool-wide duplication is a term in that floor.

claims.text: Reader-pool dispatch stickiness — starting `ReaderPool._dispatch`'s scan at the slot that served the previous read rather than the next one — is worth a reproduced -32.2% on a statement's first four executions, -21.8% on its first eight and -13.2% on its first thirty-two, decaying to -1.6% by the eight-thousandth. In absolute terms four sequential point reads of a fresh statement fall from 58 us to 39 us, and the saving is dominated by a term paid once per statement rather than by a per-read rate: ~19 us across the first four executions, ~22 us across the first eight, ~30 us across the first thirty-two. The mechanism accounts for the magnitude — round-robin makes all four reader connections prepare the statement, build its schema and warm its pages, so the candidate avoids three cycles of roughly 6-9 us each, and the percentage falls because an increasing execution count is what it is divided by. Twenty-four alternating-order lane-isolated AOT passes in two collections of twelve, 121 samples per lane per arm; all 24 passes were faster on `first4-newsql` and `first8-newsql`, 22 of 24 were faster on `first32-newsql`, and the shipped-code collection classified all 12 `first4`/`first8` pass-pairs plus four of six `first32` pairs as REPRODUCED. The other two `first32` pairs reversed sign across the order flip and were marked drift-suspected by `ab_drift_check.dart`.

claims.text: A fixed per-(statement, worker) cost is structurally invisible to resqlite's benchmark suite, and this is a property of the suite rather than of any one lane. Every release scenario and every focused harness lane executes one statement from tens to thousands of times per sample, because that is what it takes to resolve a per-read effect at microsecond scale; a cost paid once per statement per worker is divided by that repeat count before it is ever reported. The discriminating instrument is a lane that mints a fresh SQL string per sample (a trailing comment leaves the plan identical) and times its first N executions. Three such lanes at N = 4, 8 and 32 bracket where the fixed term stops mattering, and the monotonic decay across them is stronger evidence for a warm-up mechanism than any single lane's magnitude.

claims.text: Two candidate per-read costs on the reader hop are refuted by direct probe and should not be attempted again without a new mechanism. First, the per-TEXT-cell `Pointer.asTypedList` view allocation in `decodeQuery`: decoding 40,000 24-byte cells through one fresh external view each costs 432 us against 378 us through a persistent window with offsets, so the view is ~1.35 ns/cell, about 1.5% of the 10k x (4 INT + 4 TEXT) read exp 251 measured at 3,587 us — and routing the bytes through a native scratch buffer to earn it would add a copy larger than the saving. Second, the per-query `RowSchema` copy across the isolate hop: an isolate ping-pong carrying a worker-cached schema (names list plus eagerly built HashMap index) against one carrying no schema at all differs by under 1% of a round trip at 6 and 21 columns and at 1, 20 and 1,000 rows — under 40 ns, indistinguishable from noise. Neither is worth an experiment.

claims.text: A dispatch-policy change can break a reclaim path that is driven by traffic, and `selectBytes` is the case in this codebase. Exp 183's `json_buf` reclaim shrinks a reader connection's serialization buffer when a later, *smaller* read arrives on that same connection; a concurrent burst of large byte reads grows all four readers' buffers, and only the round-robin rotation brings the settling small reads back round to reclaim them. Making every read sticky left the three workers a burst had grown unvisited, and `Diagnostics.readerJsonBufHighWaterBytes` settled at 6.2 MB against the 512 KB the exp 185 release guard allows — a real retention regression that the wall-time harness could not see and the guard caught on its first run. `selectBytes` therefore keeps the pre-266 rotation while `select` sticks. The boundary is structural rather than expedient: the bytes path retains a per-connection buffer whose reclaim is traffic-driven, and the rows path retains nothing per connection. Pinned by a `selectBytes keeps rotating` unit test and by the `bytes-first8-newsql` harness lane, which reads -1.2% (7 of 12 passes faster) as an unchanged path should.

nextSignals: `benchmark/experiments/reader_dispatch_stickiness.dart` is the durable gate for any future change to *which* worker serves a read, and its `first{4,8,32}-newsql` lanes are reusable well beyond this experiment: they are the only lanes in the repo that can see a fixed per-statement cost at all. Any future candidate whose saving is paid once per statement — statement-cache sizing, schema-cache capacity, connection setup, prepare cost — should be measured there before a steady-state lane is allowed to call it neutral.

Traffic-driven reclaim paths are now a named hazard for any future dispatch or routing change. `json_buf` is the one that exists today (exp 183's shrink needs a later small read on the *same* connection), and it was invisible to a wall-time harness — the `JSON buffer reclaim` release guard is what caught it. Before changing which worker serves which read again, enumerate the per-connection state that only shrinks when that connection is used, and run `dart test test/benchmark_sqlite_diagnostics_test.dart` early rather than at the end.

The same stickiness question is open on two paths this experiment deliberately did not touch. Stream re-queries go through `ReaderPool.select` and `selectIfChanged` and therefore already inherit it, but a stream's re-query is issued once per invalidation against a statement that stays hot, so it sits in the steady-state regime where the effect is ~0; whether a *fan-out* of many distinct stream statements behaves like `alternating-sql` (neutral) or like `first8-newsql` (a win) has not been measured and is the natural follow-up in `stream-rerun-dispatch`. `selectBytes` shares the dispatch path unchanged.

The pool now concentrates warm state on one connection by default, which changes what the per-connection caps mean. Each reader connection has its own 32-entry C statement cache, its own 32-entry Dart `schemaCache`, and `cache_size = -8192` (8 MB) of page cache. Under round-robin an application with many distinct statements thrashed all four caches identically; under stickiness it thrashes one hard and leaves three cold. That is the correct trade for the measured shape and it is untested at the tail — a workload with well over 32 hot statements might now evict where it previously did not. The cheap discriminating lane is `first8-newsql` widened to rotate more distinct statements than a connection can cache.

The reader pool's `_preferred` cursor is the second piece of main-isolate-held per-read policy, after exp 260/264's `_rowHints`. Both are cheap and both are invisible from any public surface, which is why each needed a test-only accessor (`rowSizeHintFor`, `preferredWorkerIndex`). If a third arrives it is probably worth a single small `ReaderPool` diagnostics view rather than a third bespoke getter.

Two preflight probes were run and thrown away, and their negative results are recorded as claim 266.4 precisely so the next runner does not rebuild them: the per-cell `asTypedList` view allocation in the TEXT decode arm (~1.35 ns/cell, ~1.5% of a text-heavy read) and the per-query `RowSchema` copy across the hop (under 1% of a round trip). Both looked like obvious waste from reading the code. Neither is.

A test that spawns its own `ReaderPool` must not exceed two workers, and the reason is host-dependent so a dev machine will not catch it. `Database.open` sizes the pool as `clamp(Platform.numberOfProcessors - 1, 2, 4)` and C allocates exactly that many reader connections; `resqlite_stmt_acquire_on` returns NULL for `reader_id >= db->reader_count`, which surfaces as `ResqliteQueryException: not an error` (no SQLite error was ever set) on the rows path and `resqlite_query_bytes failed with code 5` on the bytes path. Exp 266's first two dispatch tests spawned four workers, passed on a ten-core dev machine and failed on a two-core CI runner. Two is the floor of the clamp and is what every pre-existing pool test already uses; if a future test genuinely needs the real width, it has to read the clamp rather than assume it.

A dispatch-policy change in the reader pool must run the stream-rerun-dispatch Tracelite preset as a guard even when its focused lanes are clean — exp 266's focused harness had conc/sacrifice/bytes guards and still had to add this post-hoc. The preset's 'inconclusive' exit is its win gate, not the guard verdict; read the per-scenario direction.

changedBeliefs: The 32-entry cap shared by the three SQL-keyed read-path caches was never a measured number, and it is a cliff rather than a slope. All three evict at the front and promote on hit, which is approximately LRU, and LRU is the worst possible policy for a cyclic scan: at D <= 32 distinct rotating statements every read hits, and at D = 33 the entry each read needs is the one the previous miss just evicted, so the hit rate collapses rather than degrading. Measured, the collapse is worth about half of every read — 14.0 us per read against 6.1 us — and it is FLAT from 40 rotating statements to 128, which is the signature of a cliff and would not be produced by gradual cache pressure.

Exp 266 moved the workload that reaches the cap by a factor of four without moving the cap. Under the round-robin dispatch it replaced, a sequential loop over D distinct statements was partitioned across the four reader connections — each cache saw roughly D/4, so a 128-statement application still fit inside 32 per connection. Sticky dispatch sends the whole cycle to one worker. This is the tail risk exp 266's own signal named ('a workload with well over 32 hot statements might now evict where it previously did not') and it is real, but it is a change in exposure, not a regression exp 266 introduced: at any D the per-cache miss rate past the cap was always total.

The cost of an eviction is O(capacity) in BYTES, not O(1), and that is what actually bounded the cache size. `stmt_cache_insert` reclaimed a slot by disposing `entries[0]` and compacting the array so the new entry landed at the tail, moving `(STMT_CACHE_MAX - 1) * sizeof(resqlite_cached_stmt)` on every prepare. At ~1.6 KB per entry (exp 248's measurement of the fixed-size `read_tables[64]` + `dep_columns[64]` arrays) that is 50 KB per prepare at 32 entries and 203 KB at 128. The first candidate raised the caps alone and measured a reproduced +42.1% on the never-reused-SQL lane — a regression large enough to reject the raise outright, on a workload no cache size can help.

The compaction bought no ordering guarantee, because `stmt_cache_lookup_entry` already promotes a hit by SWAPPING it with the tail rather than shifting. Entry order was therefore only approximate before the change and is only approximate after it. Reclaiming the LRU slot in place — new entry at the front, where the next eviction takes it unless something looks it up first — took the guard lane from +42.1% to a reproduced -11.9%, because the 32-entry baseline was already paying ~640 us of its 3688 us sample to shift 12.8 MB. A per-prepare cost that scaled with capacity was the reason the capacity question looked closed, and it was never the capacity's cost.

The memory price of the raise is small and it is not where intuition puts it. Peak RSS rises 0.8-1.2 MB against a ~30 MB floor for 128 entries across the writer, four readers and the reserved reader; SQLite's own `Stmt` accounting rises 70.5 -> 103.4 KiB on the release suite's 48-distinct-statement diagnostics section. What makes even that price avoidable is the entry shape: `read_tables[64]` (512 B) and `dep_columns[64]` (1 KB) are fixed-size arrays sized for a worst case, and a typical statement reads one table and a handful of columns.

The repo already had a workload past the cliff and could not see it. `benchmark/suites/sqlite_diagnostics.dart` runs 48 distinct SELECT texts in its `Statement cache footprint` section — 50% past the old cap — but it reports memory, not time, so it recorded the consequence of total statement-cache thrash as a footprint number for months without anyone reading it as a latency signal.

claims.text: Raising the three SQL-keyed read-path caps (`STMT_CACHE_MAX`, `_schemaCacheMax`, `ReaderPool.rowSizeMemoryMax`) from 32 to 128, together with in-place LRU-slot reclaim in `stmt_cache_insert`, is worth a reproduced -55.5% at 40 rotating distinct statements, -55.1% at 64 and -53.3% at 128, on a lane issuing 256 point reads per sample. Per read that is 14.0 us -> 6.1 us. The win is flat across 40-128 statements, which is the cliff signature; every lane inside the old cap (`rotate8`, `rotate24`, `rotate32`, `point1`) is neutral in two independent order-flipped collections, and peak RSS rises 0.8-1.2 MB.

nextSignals: `benchmark/experiments/stmt_cache_pressure.dart` is the workload exps 071 and 073 each asked for and neither built, and it is now the durable gate for any change to a SQL-keyed cache: capacity, eviction policy, lookup cost, or entry layout. Its lane roles are worth preserving as they are — `rotate8`/`rotate24` inside the cap, `rotate32` on it, `rotate{40,64,128}` past it, and `churn-unique` where no cache can help. The last of those is the only lane in the repo that can reject a cache from getting bigger, and it did exactly that once already.

The cliff moves to 128; it does not disappear. An application with more than 128 hot statements lands in the state this run found at 33, and nothing measures where a real statement mix sits. This is the same measurement exp 264's signal named (count distinct SQL strings per second in a representative trace against the cap) and it is now worth more: it bounds a 2x cliff rather than a 40% hint.

The named follow-up is the entry, not the cap. `resqlite_cached_stmt` is ~1.6 KB almost entirely because `read_tables[64]` (512 B) and `dep_columns[64]` (1 KB) are fixed-size arrays sized for a worst case that a typical statement — one table, a handful of columns — does not approach. Sizing them from what the authorizer actually captured would shrink a common entry by roughly an order of magnitude, which would make a further capacity raise nearly free, shorten the linear scan that is the remaining `churn-unique` cost, and reduce the pool footprint exp 263 identified as where resqlite's memory actually sits. It adds a malloc per prepare, which is off the hot path by construction.

The front-insert eviction was chosen because it removes an O(capacity) cost, not because its hit rate was compared against the compacting version at equal capacity. The two are indistinguishable on every lane here — below the cap neither evicts, above it a cyclic workload defeats both — so if a future run builds a non-cyclic over-capacity workload (a hot working set plus a cold tail, say), the policy comparison is still open and the harness already has the shape to host it.

A cache-sizing change needs a negative control on its tests, and it is cheap to build. Every test here passed on the first run, which proves nothing about a cache that fails silently; installing a deliberately mismatched entry took one rebuild and showed four of the five tests catch it. Any future test whose failure mode is 'plausible data from the wrong slot' should be verified this way before it is trusted.

`benchmark/suites/sqlite_diagnostics.dart`'s `Statement cache footprint` section runs 48 distinct SELECT texts and has therefore been sitting past the old cliff for months, reporting it as a footprint number rather than a latency one. Its `Stmt` KiB reading moves 70.5 -> 103.4 with this change, which is the expected direction; it is a reporting section, not a gate, so nothing fails, but a reader comparing footprints across this merge boundary should know the cause.

changedBeliefs: Exp 267's measured +0.8-1.2 MB statement-cache RSS was real, but most of the four-reader price was not retained prepared statements or populated dependency metadata. `resqlite_db` comes from `calloc`, then `stmt_cache_init` wrote the complete 128-entry array again; optimized arm64 removed that redundant write for the adjacent writer cache but retained a 273,408-byte `bzero` for every reader. Four readers therefore eagerly touched 1,093,632 bytes before any cache slot became live. Removing that clear recovers 1,056,768 bytes of median max RSS, almost the whole observation that named dynamic metadata as the next target.

The native statement-cache entry is 2,136 bytes, not the approximate 1.6 KB carried from exp 248 into exp 267. `resqlite_column_dep` is 24 bytes, so `dep_columns[64]` alone occupies 1,536 bytes; one 128-entry cache is exactly 273,408 bytes (`0x42c00`). The corrected size strengthens exp 267's eviction-compaction explanation but changes the footprint follow-up: unused capacity can stay virtual without changing entry ownership at all.

A count-bounded inline array has an explicit publication boundary. `stmt_cache_lookup_entry` and `stmt_cache_clear` inspect only `[0, count)`, while `stmt_cache_insert` fully zeroes the selected slot through `stmt_cache_entry_init` before incrementing count. Under that invariant, clearing capacity at container construction is not defensive initialization; it is an eager page-fault policy. The 400-statement eviction suite and dependency-reliability tests remain green because every live and recycled slot still takes the same full initialization path.

A source-level `calloc` argument is insufficient evidence that unused capacity stays non-resident. Dead-store elimination differed by placement inside one function: the compiler removed the writer-cache clear adjacent to `calloc` and retained the identical reader-cache clear inside the connection-open loop. The durable attribution paired optimized assembly with two- and four-reader fresh-process RSS; source inspection alone would have predicted either all clears or no clears and missed the actual binary.

Dynamic dependency metadata is no longer the first-order response to exp 267's memory number. It may still shrink a populated 128-entry cache and make a future capacity raise cheaper, but it adds one or two allocations per prepare, failure-conservative reliability semantics, fragmentation and disposal ownership. After empty capacity stays virtual, that complexity needs a representative filled-cache or >128-statement trace; empty-open RSS cannot justify it.

nextSignals: `benchmark/experiments/stmt_cache_init.dart` is the durable gate for changes to connection-open native footprint. Keep both `rss2` and `rss4`: one fresh process per lane gives an absolute observation, while the reader-count slope discriminates a per-reader cache mechanism from the Dart process floor and writer-side work. Pair max RSS with the lane's start-to-peak growth; neither is a byte-exact allocator counter.

Inspect optimized code before attributing a large `calloc`-backed structure's resident footprint. A nested initializer can fault every page again even when the parent begins zeroed, and the compiler can eliminate one call site while retaining another. The minimum proof is the live-range invariant, a binary-level check that the write exists, and a cardinality sweep (reader count here) that scales the measured memory.

Exact-sized `read_tables` / `dep_columns` storage remains open only for populated-cache footprint. Gate it on `point1`, `rotate128` and `churn-unique` AOT pressure lanes, the 400-statement correctness suite, overflow/OOM reliability tests, and a representative workload that actually fills many entries. Empty-open RSS has been consumed and cannot support the added allocations.

Exp 267's approximate 1.6 KB entry size should not be reused in new arithmetic. The current layout is 2,136 bytes and the exact cache array is 273,408 bytes at 128 entries; remeasure `sizeof(resqlite_cached_stmt)` whenever dependency fields or cached JSON metadata change.
