This experiment does not add risk there because each recycled slot is still memset before use, but the next change to entry ownership or disposal should add that over-capacity token-reuse case before claiming all fields are eviction-gated.

changedBeliefs: Exp 269 strengthens rather than supersedes exp 265's rejection. Row, payload-byte and VM-opcode caps still do not bound caller-isolate wall time: arbitrary work can occur inside one SQLite opcode, before the progress handler is installed, or while SQLite is waiting below the VM. The missing primitive is preemption, not a better predictor or another counter.

changedBeliefs: We believed resqlite's write-invalidation signal was a general-purpose fact about the database, used so far only by streams. It is not: it is a fact about writes made through one `Database` object. Streams can live with that because a missed invalidation only delays a re-emit, and `stream()` documents the limitation. `select()` cannot, because it re-reads the file today and therefore observes every committed write, whoever made it. Anyone reading the stream-engine chapters or the invalidation sections of the architecture doc should read 'invalidation' as scoped to this Database's own writes, not to the file.

The round-trip headroom exp 265 priced and exp 269 confirmed is collectable without running SQLite on the caller. A cache hit measured 0.48 us against a 4.65 us dispatched point read, reproduced at -90% to -96% across four lanes and two order-flipped collections, with every adversarial guard neutral and peak RSS flat or lower. The blocker is not performance and not the bounding problem exp 269 hit; it is that the invalidation signal has the wrong scope.

The cost of a cache is paid on the write path, and that is where an invalidation design should be judged first. A table-to-queries index with column-level elision — the shape the stream engine uses — measured +16-19% on a read/write-alternating lane, because a write pays it whether or not anything is cached. Replacing it with per-table version counters checked at lookup moved the whole cost onto the reader that benefits and took the same lane to neutral.

The release suite cannot evaluate a read cache. Its read scenarios execute one statement thousands of times with nothing writing, so `Select -> Maps` at 100 rows reports 0.040 ms -> 0.005 ms and the number is the benchmark measuring itself. This is exp 267's observation (every benchmark in the repo uses under ten distinct SQL strings) on a new axis, and it generalises: any candidate keyed on statement identity needs a workload that mixes reads with writes to what they read.

A first incidence number now exists for read repetition. Across the repo's two application-shaped workloads, Chat Sim (A5) would serve 17.7% of 9,006 `select()` calls from cache and Feed Paging (A6) 84.3% of 140 — a near-5x spread between two workloads in the same repository, so the value of remembering a read is a property of how much a workload writes to what it reads, not a constant. changedBeliefs: We believed the admission half of exp 265's round-trip price (claim 265.2) was unreachable without moving SQLite to the calling isolate, because the three experiments that attacked it — 265, 269, 270 — all did so by removing the worker. That is now false as a statement about mechanism: scheduling the wait rather than removing it collects 75-86% of a point read's latency behind a saturated pool, with no caller-isolate SQLite, no staleness contract and no starvation. A reader of exps 265/269/270 should stop treating 'the pool is busy' latency as intrinsically coupled to the transport question; it is a scheduling property and it is separable.

We also believed, without ever measuring it, that reader-pool queueing is a real cost on real workloads — the premise under exps 105, 114, 118, 120, 239 and 249 and under this one. It is not, at the pool's shipped width. One full release-suite pass measured 335,221 dispatches, 325,909 of them cheap by a 64-row classifier, 312 cheap reads that parked at all, and zero that parked behind a costly waiter. Exps 118 and 120 reported dispatcherParkedTotal at zero for stream workloads specifically; the general statement is stronger and it is what closes this experiment. Anyone reading those experiments as 'streams stopped parking the dispatcher' should read them instead as 'four workers exceed what these workloads ask for at once'.

The reservation arm's rejection is the fourth instance of one pattern, and the pattern should now be assumed rather than rediscovered. Exps 197, 213, 239 and 249 each proved a mechanism and each died because the mechanism silently spent one caller's cost on another's benefit. Exp 275's reservation buys point-read latency with a reproduced +47 to +63% on four concurrent large reads. A reader of any of those five writeups should treat 'hidden policy that reallocates cost between callers' as rejected by default, and require an explicit caller-visible mode before measuring it.

Exp 265's `point-under-load` lane is not a reusable measurement for admission work and its methodology passage should not be copied. It sums ten point reads issued after the pool is saturated, but sticky dispatch (exp 266) puts reads two through ten on a worker that has already freed, so nine of the ten measure an idle pool in every arm. That was correct for exp 265, whose candidate removed all ten from the pool, and wrong for anything that changes only who waits: measured that way this candidate read -13% instead of -75%.

Exp 239's stated reopen condition — 'a reliable private cost signal' — has been satisfiable since exps 260/264 shipped RowSizeMemory.highWater, and nobody noticed because the signal was built in a different direction for buffer sizing. It is available on the dispatch fast path, one line above the worker scan, and classifying a statement from it costs nothing measurable. Future readers of exp 239 should know the blocker it named is gone; what remains blocking is incidence, which is a different objection.

claims.text: Reader-pool admission ordering has effectively zero incidence on the repo's representative workloads. One full `benchmark/run_release.dart --repeat=1` pass — chat sim, feed paging, concurrent reads 4x/8x, streaming fan-out, keyed-PK subscriptions, diagnostics and memory scenarios — recorded 335,221 reader dispatches, of which 325,909 (97.2%) were cheap by a 64-row per-SQL high-water classifier. Only 312 cheap dispatches (0.096% of cheap) parked for a worker at all, and 0 parked while any costly request was already waiting. claims.text: A last-free-worker reservation needs no per-request denial cap to stay live, and adding one silently defeats it. changedBeliefs: We believed that trimming Dart's async plumbing off resqlite's hot paths was a candidate whose size was unknown and whose measurement was the hard part. Exp 171 put one `await` on an already-resolved future at "~1-2 us per call" and derived 6-12% of headroom on a 2,000-call write burst from that estimate, then found nothing and concluded its harness was too coarse. We now believe the estimate was the error, not the harness: that hop prices at 70.7 ns and a forwarding `async` frame at 34.6 ns, so exp 171's figure was 14-28x too large and the headroom it went looking for never existed. Claim 278.1 supersedes claim 171.1 — which this run had to mint from exp 171's own changedBeliefs before it could edge to it — and the conclusion exp 171 reached survives its arithmetic being replaced.

We believed the open question about the read prologue was 'can any harness resolve it'. It is now closed by division rather than by measurement. The whole prologue on `Database.select` -> `ReaderPool.select` -> `ReaderPool._dispatch` is 142.7 ns, of which a candidate removes ~108 ns; against a 5.4 us point read that is 2.0%, against a 1,000-row read 0.05%, and the gate is 5%. No implementation of the idea reaches the gate, so the reopen conditions are a numerator change (an SDK where async frames get materially dearer) or a denominator change (a read path an order of magnitude cheaper, which means the isolate round trip is gone rather than trimmed). 'Retry on a quieter host' is explicitly not a reopen condition, and the next runner in this family should start with `async_prologue_price.dart` rather than a candidate.

`dart run tool/knowledge/impact.dart origin/main` reports nothing retired and no documented passage standing on moved ground: 171.1 appears only because this run minted it, and the supersession replaces a figure no chapter ever quoted. Nothing in `doc/arch/` needs a rewrite. What does change for a reader is exp 171's writeup itself — its Hypothesis section's "at ~1-2 µs per hop" arithmetic is now known to be wrong by more than an order of magnitude, and anyone reading it for the size of the opportunity should read claim 278.1 instead. `experiments/index/171.json` carries `amendedBy: 278` so the README shows the lineage; the verdict on that row is unchanged and correct.

A third belief, about instruments rather than about async: we treated guard lanes and control lanes as the same thing. They are not. `mixed6-10k` in this run has a computable ceiling of 0.004% and it read -2.9% pooled, which is what made `point1`'s pooled -3.0% legible as apparatus rather than effect. A guard lane answers 'did anything break'; a control lane whose arithmetic ceiling is near zero answers 'what can this collection resolve at all', and without the second one this run would have reported a 3% win it did not have.

claims.text: Dart's async plumbing is a nanosecond-scale cost, not a microsecond-scale one, and resqlite's read prologue is priced accordingly. Measured with no SQLite, no isolates and no resqlite code — a sync completer resolved from a separate microtask, reached through four amounts of plumbing, five AOT runs of 21 samples x 200,000 calls: awaiting an already-resolved future before the real one costs 70.7 ns, and each `async` function that only forwards a future costs 34.6 ns. The prologue `Database.select` -> `ReaderPool.select` -> `ReaderPool._dispatch` -> `_WorkerSlot.request` therefore carried 142.7 ns over a direct await, of which a candidate that makes `Database.select`, `Database.selectBytes` and `_dispatch`'s first scan non-async removes ~108 ns. Divided by what it wraps that is 2.0% of a 5.4 us point read, 1.1% of a 20-row page, 0.05% of a 1,000-row read and 0.004% of a sacrificed 10,000-row one — a ceiling below the 5% decision gate on every shape resqlite measures, so no implementation of the idea can clear it. Exp 171 estimated the same resolved-future hop at 1-2 us per call and derived 6-12% of headroom from that estimate; the figure is 14-28x too large and the headroom never existed.

279.outcomeNote: The candidate transport is slower than the one it was meant to replace, at every payload size and end to end, so the vehicle question closes rather than staying open. Runtime reverted; prototype at `archive/exp-279`; the isolate-only lanes are retained as `benchmark/experiments/isolate_transport_price.dart`.
changedBeliefs: We believed the isolate round trip's 6.3 us (claim 265.1) was the price of keeping SQLite off the calling isolate, and that the four rejections since — unbounded caller work (265.6), unbounded opaque SQLite work (269.2), foreign-writer staleness (exp 270), zero incidence (275.1) — were each about a consequence of removing the worker rather than about the hop itself. That framing left the hop looking collectable by anyone who solved the safety problem. We now believe it is not collectable at all by changing vehicles: a POSIX worker thread, which gives the caller identical protection, costs 4.28 us per round trip parked on a condvar and 3.18 us spinning, against 1.46 us for a Dart isolate. The Dart VM's same-group message path is the cheapest available way to get work off the calling isolate and an answer back, and a future runner should stop looking for a better one.

We believed — implicitly, because nobody had split it — that most of the 6.3 us hop was messages. It is not: a point read's whole transport, request object out and result shape back, is 3.22 us. The other half is resqlite's own per-request work on the two sides of the messages, and a perfect zero-cost transport would leave it standing. Claim 279.3 refines claim 265.1 rather than replacing it: the 6.3 us is still right as the price of the hop, but it is now decomposed, and the half worth attacking is the one nobody has measured. Anyone reading exp 265 for where to aim next should read 279.3 beside it.

We believed exp 174's view-send was right because it avoided a `Uint8List.fromList` copy. The measurement says the reason is larger than that and worth stating on its own: the VM charges for a payload's *backing*, not its size. Byte-for-byte identical 256 KB sends in 9.01 us as a view over malloc'd memory and 43.06 us as a heap `Uint8List` — 4.8x. Claim 279.4 validates claim 174.1 with the number it was reasoned from, and it now constrains anything future: a path that assembles bytes on the Dart heap before sending them pays roughly five times the transfer, and nothing downstream of the send recovers it.

`dart run tool/knowledge/impact.dart origin/main` reports nothing retired and no documented passage standing on moved ground. 265.1 is refined rather than superseded, so the figure every writeup quotes stays correct; 174.1 is validated. `doc/arch/cross-isolate-data-transfer.md` is the one passage a reader should revisit — not because anything in it is now wrong, but because §6a's send-vs-sacrifice account is where the backing-vs-size result belongs alongside exp 245's copy-per-slot rule, and a future edit should put it there.

claims.text: Running a read on a native POSIX thread instead of a Dart reader isolate is slower, not faster, and the primitive is not the reason. An awaited Dart isolate round trip costs 1.46 us; handing the same job to a worker thread and getting an answer back through `Dart_PostCObject_DL` costs 4.28 us parked on a condvar and 3.18 us with the worker spinning on the queue (a burned core, included so the result cannot be blamed on the wake primitive). End to end against a real database the same shape holds: `db.selectBytes()` on one row is 5.48 us against 6.43 us for the native worker (+17.3%), at 1,000 rows 246.5 against 249.3 (+1.1%), and at 5,000 rows 1239 against 1233 (-0.5%, inside the floor). Native dispatch is never faster at any size. The vehicle question is therefore closed: keeping SQLite off the calling isolate does not cost extra because a Dart isolate was chosen.

claims.text: The 2-3 us by which native dispatch loses is the cross-thread wake, not the native port. A post issued from the calling thread itself, so the main isolate never sleeps between issuing and receiving, costs 0.67 us — `Dart_PostCObject_DL` delivery plus one event-loop turn. Everything above that in the native lanes is the OS scheduling round trip, and the Dart VM performs the equivalent handoff in both directions for 1.46 us. This is the number that makes the rejection conditional rather than permanent: a runtime or SDK where a foreign thread can wake a sleeping isolate cheaply would change the arithmetic, and nothing else in the mechanism would have to change.

claims.text: A point read's cross-isolate transport is 3.22 us — about half of claim 265.1's 6.3 us hop. Measured with no SQLite and no resqlite code, one persistent echo isolate, changing only what crosses the boundary: an int each way is 1.46 us, a `SelectRequest`-shaped object outbound adds 0.50 us, a point read's reply shape inbound (one row of six cells, six column names, the `(result, sacrificed, error)` envelope, pre-built on the worker) adds 1.74 us, and both together in one trip are 3.22 us — less than the 3.70 us the parts sum to, because some of what each shape costs is per-trip rather than per-payload, which is why the combined lane exists. The remaining ~3.1 us of the hop is resqlite's own per-request work on the two sides of the messages — pool bookkeeping and the row-size memory lookup, request construction, the worker's `setBusy` bracket and request dispatch, the completion handler chain, blob materialization — none of which a transport change touches. Any future candidate in this direction should be aimed at that half; the messages have at most 3.22 us in them.

claims.text: What `SendPort.send` charges for a bulk payload is its backing, not its size. Byte-for-byte identical 256 KB costs 9.01 us to send as a view over malloc'd memory and 43.06 us as an ordinary heap `Uint8List` — 4.8x, reproduced in every pass of two collections with the two lanes differing in nothing else. This is the measurement behind exp 174's choice to send a `Uint8List` view over the reader's persistent `json_buf` rather than materialize the result first, and it generalises past `selectBytes`: any path that assembles bytes on the Dart heap before sending them pays roughly five times the transfer. It is the bulk-payload counterpart to claim 245.1's copy-per-slot rule for result structure.

claims.text: Copying is a wash between the two transports, so external typed data buys only what it saves by not copying at all — and that variant is not implementable. A malloc plus a 256 KB `memcpy` on the native side costs 6.28 us (`nport-bytes` 11.91 minus `nport-bytes-nocopy` 5.63); the VM's copy of the same view costs 7.55 us (`iso-bytes` 9.01 minus `iso-echo` 1.46). The realistic native variant therefore loses by 2.90 us, which is its dispatch penalty and nothing else. Posting the buffer itself with no copy is 3.38 us faster than the shipped path, but making that real means handing `json_buf` to the main isolate and giving the connection a fresh one, forfeiting the buffer reuse exp 174 measured as decisive (a `NativeFinalizer` zero-copy transfer was 14-24% slower at every size) and the shrink-and-reclaim policy exp 183 built on it. The prize is 1.4% of a 1,000-row `selectBytes` against a fixed dispatch tax on every small read.

nextSignals: Do not propose another transport for the read path. Exps 265, 269, 270 and 275 removed the worker four different ways and were each rejected on a consequence; exp 279 kept the worker and changed what it is, and the replacement is 2.2-2.9x more expensive. The only reopen condition is claim 279.2's numerator: an SDK or platform where a foreign thread can wake a sleeping isolate for materially less than ~2 us. Re-run the archived prototype at `archive/exp-279` against `isolate_transport_price.dart` before assuming otherwise.

The next candidate in this direction should target the half of claim 265.1 that is not transport. Claim 279.3 puts a point read's messages at 3.22 us of the 6.3 us hop, leaving ~3.1 us in per-request work that no transport change reaches: `ReaderPool._dispatch`'s row-hint lookup and stamping, request object construction, the worker's `resqliteReaderSetBusy` bracket and request-type dispatch, `_WorkerSlot`'s completion handler chain, `_record`, and `blobTransfer.materializeCells`. None of these has ever been measured individually and several are plausibly sub-microsecond, so the first step is a decomposition, not a candidate.

`benchmark/experiments/isolate_transport_price.dart` is the ruler for anything that changes what crosses the isolate boundary. It needs no database, no native code and no isolate pool, runs in seconds, and prices request shape, reply shape and bulk payload separately. Run it before proposing a message-shape change — including any revival of columnar transfer (exps 055, 081, 251, 258) — and divide by the read it wraps.

Claim 279.4 is a constraint on future design, not just a finding: a bulk payload's Dart backing decides its send cost, at 4.8x for 256 KB. Any candidate that would build a `Uint8List` on the Dart heap before sending it — a worker-side decode, a re-encode, a concatenation of chunks — pays that multiple, and the fix is always to keep the bytes native and send a view.
